title: Does OSHA require annual fire extinguisher training?
description: OSHA 1910.157(g) fire extinguisher training: education at hire and annually, designated fire fighters, and the evacuation exemptions, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: Yes, where portable fire extinguishers are provided for employee use. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) standard 29 CFR 1910.157(g) requires an educational program on the general principles of extinguisher use and the hazards of incipient stage fire fighting, given upon initial employment and at least annually. Employees designated to use fire fighting equipment under an emergency action plan need hands-on training in that equipment at initial assignment and at least annually.
keyTakeaways: The duty depends on a policy choice: paragraph (g)(1) applies where the employer has provided portable fire extinguishers for employee use in the workplace.
General education is required at initial employment and at least annually under 1910.157(g)(2).
Employees designated to fight fires under an emergency action plan need training in the appropriate equipment at initial assignment and at least annually under (g)(3) and (g)(4).
An employer with a written total evacuation policy, a compliant emergency action plan and fire prevention plan, and no extinguishers available is exempt from the whole section under (b)(1).
Hose stations used instead of Class A extinguishers require employees to be trained at least annually in their use under (d)(3).
jurisdiction: United States (federal, with state plan variations)
regulator: Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA), US Department of Labor
appliesTo: General industry employers that provide portable fire extinguishers for employee use, including offices, warehouses, retail, manufacturing and healthcare facilities
All employees in workplaces where extinguishers are provided for employee use
Employees designated to use fire fighting equipment as part of an emergency action plan

sections.heading: When does OSHA's fire extinguisher training requirement apply?

blocks.text: The training requirement applies when portable fire extinguishers are provided for employee use. [29 CFR 1910.157](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.157) covers the placement, use, maintenance and testing of portable extinguishers "provided for the use of employees" (paragraph (a)), and paragraph (g)(1) ties the educational program to the same condition. The employer's fire response policy therefore decides which training obligations apply.
Three policy options produce three different training outcomes:

sections.heading: What must fire extinguisher education cover?

blocks.text: The education must familiarize employees with two things: the general principles of fire extinguisher use, and the hazards involved with incipient stage fire fighting. Paragraph (g)(1) is short and does not list sub-topics, so the employer designs the content.

The rest of the section suggests what that content should include. Paragraph (d)(1) requires extinguishers to be selected and distributed based on the classes of anticipated workplace fires, with maximum travel distances of 75 feet for Class A and 50 feet for Class B hazards under (d)(2) and (d)(4). Employees should therefore learn which fire classes their area presents, where the nearest suitable extinguisher is, and when a fire has grown past the incipient stage and evacuation is the only safe choice. Paragraph (c)(3) prohibits extinguishers using carbon tetrachloride or chlorobromomethane, which is a useful point for anyone bringing older equipment on site.

blocks.title: Education is not the same as training
blocks.text: Paragraph (g)(1) uses the word education and (g)(3) uses the word training. The general workforce must be familiarized with principles and hazards. Designated fire fighting employees must be trained in the use of the appropriate equipment, which implies practical skill, not just awareness.

sections.heading: How often must fire extinguisher training be given?

blocks.text: Both tiers are annual. Paragraph (g)(2) requires the general education "upon initial employment and at least annually thereafter", and (g)(4) requires designated employees' training "upon initial assignment to the designated group of employees and at least annually thereafter."

A third annual duty applies where hose systems replace extinguishers. Under (d)(3), an employer may use uniformly spaced standpipe systems or hose stations connected to a sprinkler system instead of Class A extinguishers, provided they meet 1910.158 or 1910.159, give total coverage, and "employees are trained at least annually in their use." Facilities that rely on hose stations need this training on the same annual calendar.

sections.heading: What extra training do designated fire fighting employees need?

blocks.text: Designated employees need training in the use of the appropriate equipment. Paragraph (g)(3) applies to employees "designated to use fire fighting equipment as part of an emergency action plan." That links the extinguisher standard to [29 CFR 1910.38](https://www.osha.gov/laws-regs/regulations/standardnumber/1910/1910.38), which sets the minimum elements of an emergency action plan, including procedures for employees who remain to operate critical plant operations and for those performing rescue or medical duties.

Under the (b)(2) exemption, the employer that names designated users and requires everyone else to evacuate immediately on the alarm is released from the distribution requirements in (d). The trade-off is that the emergency action plan must clearly name who is designated, and those people must carry current annual training. A designated employee whose training has lapsed weakens the basis for the exemption. The emergency action plan duties are covered in [OSHA emergency action plan training requirements](/regulations/osha-emergency-action-plan-training-requirements).

sections.heading: What evidence shows fire extinguisher training is compliant?

blocks.text: Paragraph (g) does not prescribe a training record. The only records in 1910.157 relate to equipment: the annual maintenance date under (e)(3), kept for one year after the last entry or the life of the shell, and hydrostatic test certification records under (f)(16). An auditor will still expect to see who was educated and when.

sections.heading: How should employers design fire extinguisher training?

blocks.text: Decide the policy first, then design the training to match. If every employee may fight an incipient fire, annual education for the whole workforce is required and the content should be site specific: the fire classes in each area, the extinguisher types mounted there, and the point at which to stop and evacuate. If only designated employees respond, invest in practical training for that group and make sure the emergency action plan names them.

Fire extinguisher education is one item in a wider set of OSHA annual cycles. See [OSHA training requirements](/regulations/osha-training-requirements) for the overview, [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) to assign the right tier to each role, and [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) for evidence that paragraph (g) leaves to the employer.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry records the employer's fire response policy as the decision that determines which training tier each role receives. If the policy changes from all employee use to designated users only, the roles affected and the content that must change are identified from that single change.

faqs.q: Is hands-on extinguisher discharge required for every employee?
faqs.a: Paragraph (g)(1) requires an educational program that familiarizes employees with general principles and the hazards of incipient stage fire fighting. It does not require every employee to discharge an extinguisher. Designated employees must be trained in the use of the appropriate equipment under (g)(3), which in practice means hands-on training.

faqs.q: Can an office avoid fire extinguisher training entirely?
faqs.a: Only under the (b)(1) exemption: a written fire safety policy requiring immediate and total evacuation on the alarm, a compliant emergency action plan and fire prevention plan, and no extinguishers available. Employees still need emergency action plan review and fire prevention information under 1910.38 and 1910.39.

faqs.q: Does the annual education need to be within 12 months of the previous session?
faqs.a: The standard says at least annually after initial employment. It does not define the interval further. A 12 month interval from each employee's previous session is the common reading and the easiest to evidence.

Section 1910.157 sits in part 1910, the general industry standards. Construction fire protection is addressed separately in part 1926, which this page does not cover. Employers with mixed operations should check which part governs each activity before setting the annual training population.

factCheck.claim: 1910.157(g)(1)-(2): educational program on general principles of extinguisher use and hazards of incipient stage fire fighting where extinguishers provided for employee use; upon initial employment and at least annually.
1910.157(g)(3)-(4): employees designated to use fire fighting equipment as part of an EAP trained in appropriate equipment upon initial assignment and at least annually.

1910.157(b)(1) total evacuation exemption with EAP and FPP and no extinguishers; (b)(2) designated user exemption from distribution requirements in (d); (a) only (e) and (f) apply where extinguishers not intended for employee use.
1910.157(d)(2) and (d)(4): travel distance 75 feet Class A, 50 feet Class B; (d)(3) hose stations instead of Class A extinguishers require employees trained at least annually.

1910.157(c)(3) carbon tetrachloride or chlorobromomethane prohibited; (e)(2) monthly visual inspection; (e)(3) annual maintenance record retained one year after last entry or life of shell; (f)(16) hydrostatic test certification records.
1910.38(c) minimum elements of EAP include procedures for employees who remain to operate critical plant operations and those performing rescue or medical duties.
